newsitem.title: USA: New plans to tighten NY-NJ airport security.
newsitem.headline: New plans to tighten NY-NJ airport security.

text.p: The operator of the New York area's three major airports announced plans on Monday to tighten security by using everything from more bomb-sniffing dogs to high-tech computer operated machines.

The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, which runs John F. Kennedy International and La Guardia airports in New York and Newark International Airport in New Jersey, said the new measures would be funded from capital and operating budgets but declined to say how much they would cost.
George Marlin, Port Authority executive director, said the agency had already met five of the 11 recommendations of the Gore Commission on airline security announced two weeks ago.

Vice President Al Gore said the recommendations for all U.S. airports included a call for better bomb detection equipment, profiling passengers, matching passengers to baggage, increased use of bomb-sniffing dogs and background checks on employees with access to secure airport areas.

President Bill Clinton, who has called on Congress to provide nearly $1.1 billion to hire more FBI agents to fight terrorism and improve airline security, asked for the Gore report after the July 17 crash of TWA Flight 800. It exploded shortly after taking off from Kennedy Airport en route to Paris, killing all 230 people on board.
The cause of the accident has not yet been determined.

"While technological advances will add to our arsenal and provide promise for the future, we agree with the Gore commission that technology itself is not a silver bullet," said Marlin, who presented a 10-point security plan for the three airports. "The front line in our defence against terrorism will always be the human element. Security is everybody's business."

Marlin said the plan called for new physical security measures, but that El Al Israel Airlines was the only carrier at Kennedy so far to receive the CTX5000 device that detects explosives in baggage with CAT-scan and computer technology.

Other measures include increased testing of security by outside experts in areas controlled by airlines and other tenants; teams of explosives-detecting dogs to start training in October and a "three-strikes-and-your-out" programme for frequent violators of airport security procedures.
